title: Arduino Uno R3
tagline: The board most people learn on: a socketed ATmega328P, 5 V pins you can't easily hurt, and a USB cable that does everything.
overview: The Uno R3 (A000066) runs an ATmega328P at 16 MHz with 5 V logic. It sits in a DIP-28 socket, so a chip you cook can be swapped in a minute. A second chip, the ATmega16U2, is the USB-to-serial bridge: it shows up as a serial port on your computer and resets the 328P when an upload starts. You get 14 digital pins (6 with PWM, marked ~), 6 analog inputs, 32 KB of flash (32 256 bytes free for your sketch after the Optiboot bootloader), 2 KB of RAM and 1 KB of EEPROM. Power it from USB, from 7-12 V on the barrel jack, or from VIN; the board switches to the jack by itself when VIN is above about 6.6 V.

mcu.atmega16u2-mu: USB-to-serial bridge. It runs Arduino's USB firmware, passes Serial in both directions and pulses the 328P's reset through C5 when an upload starts.

usb.protection: F1, a 500 mA resettable polyfuse, sits between USB and the board. A short trips it; it cools and resets by itself.

jack.protection: D1 (an M7 diode) blocks a reversed adapter, and drops about 0.7 V on the way to VIN.

vin.protection: None. The VIN pin is after D1, so a reversed supply here goes straight into the regulator and its capacitor.

pin5.protection: None. Feeding the 5V pin skips the regulator, the polyfuse and every protection on the board: it must be a clean 5 V.

rails.5v: Made by U1 (NCP1117) from VIN, or passed through from USB by T1 when VIN is below about 6.6 V.
rails.3v3: Made by U2 (LP2985) from 5 V. 150 mA at most, for small sensors only.
rails.vin: The jack voltage less D1's drop: about 8.3 V from a 9 V adapter.
rails.usbvcc: USB's 5 V after the polyfuse. It feeds the 16U2 and, through T1, the 5 V rail.

power.io: 20 mA per pin is a safe design limit and 40 mA is the absolute maximum. All pins together must stay under 200 mA.

iol.1: RX. Also wired to the 16U2 through a 1 kΩ resistor: anything on D0 can block uploads.
iol.2: TX. Serial.print() sends its bytes out here, and the 16U2 passes them to USB.
iol.3: External interrupt 0: attachInterrupt() works on D2 and D3 only.
iol.4: PWM at 490 Hz and external interrupt 1. tone() borrows the same timer, so PWM here stops while a tone plays.
iol.8: The last pin of the left header; then the gap that makes Uno shields fit only one way.

ioh.2: PWM at 490 Hz. The Servo library takes over this timer, so analogWrite() on D9 and D10 stops working once a servo is attached.
ioh.3: PWM, and SPI SS. It must stay an output while the Uno is the SPI master.
ioh.6: Built-in LED pin (LED_BUILTIN). The L LED hangs off it through a buffer, so it does not load the pin.
ioh.8: Reference for analogRead(). Leave it alone unless you call analogReference(EXTERNAL) first.
ioh.9: I²C data. The same wire as A4: use one or the other.
ioh.10: I²C clock. The same wire as A5.

power.1: Not connected: kept free for future shields.
power.2: Tells a shield the board's I/O voltage: 5 V on the Uno.
power.3: Pull it to GND to reset the 328P, the same as the RESET button.
power.5: 5 V out from the board. You can also feed a clean 5 V in here, but nothing protects the board if you get it wrong.
power.8: The jack's voltage after D1, or a 7-12 V input that skips D1's protection.

ad.1: Analog input 0. Like A1-A5 it also works as a digital pin (D14).
ad.5: Analog input 4 and I²C SDA: the same pin as SDA on the top header.
ad.6: Analog input 5 and I²C SCL: the same pin as SCL on the top header.

icsp.5: The 328P's reset line, for an in-circuit programmer.

icsp1.5: The 16U2's reset. Briefly joining it to GND (pin 6) puts the 16U2 in its DFU bootloader.

leds.ON: Lit whenever the 5 V rail is up.
leds.L: Follows D13: lit when D13 is HIGH. It flashes three times when the bootloader starts after a reset.
leds.TX: Flickers when the board sends serial data to the computer.
leds.RX: Flickers when the computer sends data to the board, including during an upload.

controls.RESET: Restarts the 328P. The bootloader flashes L three times, waits about a second for an upload, then runs your sketch from the top.

ZU4.name: ATmega328P microcontroller
ZU4.what: The chip that runs your sketch: 8-bit AVR, 16 MHz, 32 KB flash, 2 KB RAM. It sits in a socket with its notch toward the ICSP header.

SK1.name: DIP-28 socket
SK1.what: Holds the 328P without soldering it, so a damaged chip comes out and a new one goes in.

U3.name: ATmega16U2 USB-to-serial bridge
U3.what: A second microcontroller that speaks USB. It turns your computer's serial port into the 328P's RX and TX, and resets the 328P for uploads.

Y1.name: 16 MHz quartz crystal
Y1.what: The 16U2's clock. USB needs a precise clock, so this one is quartz.

Y2.name: 16 MHz ceramic resonator
Y2.what: The 328P's clock. Less precise than quartz but plenty for a sketch; without it the 328P does not run at all.

U1.name: NCP1117 5 V regulator
U1.what: Turns 7-12 V from the jack or VIN into 5 V. With 12 V in and a big 5 V load it gets very hot.

U2.name: LP2985 3.3 V regulator
U2.what: Makes the 3V3 pin's 3.3 V from 5 V, 150 mA at most.

U5.name: LMV358 dual op-amp
U5.what: One half compares VIN with 3.3 V to choose between USB and the jack; the other half buffers D13 for the L LED.

T1.name: FDN340P MOSFET
T1.what: The USB power switch. It passes USB's 5 V to the board until VIN rises above about 6.6 V.

F1.name: 500 mA polyfuse
F1.what: A resettable fuse on USB's 5 V. A short makes it hot and high-resistance; it recovers once it cools.

D1.name: M7 protection diode
D1.what: Lets current from the barrel jack in only one direction, so a reversed adapter does nothing.

D2.name: 328P reset clamp diode
D2.what: Stops the auto-reset pulse from pushing the RESET pin above 5 V.

D3.name: 16U2 reset clamp diode
D3.what: The same clamp, on the 16U2's reset line.

PC1.name: 47 µF capacitor on VIN
PC1.what: Smooths the input supply. It is polarised: the black band marks the negative end.

PC2.name: 47 µF capacitor on 5 V
PC2.what: Holds the 5 V rail steady when the load jumps. Polarised, like PC1.

L1.name: Ferrite bead
L1.what: Joins the USB socket's metal shield to ground and keeps high-frequency noise out.

L2.name: 10 µH inductor
L2.what: Filters the 5 V that feeds the 328P's analog section (AVCC), for quieter analogRead() values.

C3.name: 1 µF capacitor
C3.what: The 3.3 V regulator's output capacitor; it needs one to stay stable.

C5.name: 100 nF auto-reset capacitor
C5.what: Turns the 16U2's DTR signal into a short reset pulse for the 328P. This is what makes one-click uploads work.

C6.name: 100 nF capacitor
C6.what: Decouples the 328P's supply pins, right beside the chip.

C8.name: 1 µF capacitor
C8.what: Stabilises the 16U2's internal USB regulator (its UCAP pin).

C9.name: 22 pF capacitor
C9.what: One of the crystal's two load capacitors.

R1.name: 1 MΩ resistor
R1.what: Across the crystal Y1, to help the oscillator start.

R2.name: 1 MΩ resistor
R2.what: Across the resonator Y2, for the same reason.

RN1.name: 10 kΩ resistor array
RN1.what: Four resistors in one part: the reset pull-ups and the divider that tells U5 what VIN is.

RN2.name: 1 kΩ resistor array
RN2.what: Current limits for the L, TX and RX LEDs.

RN3.name: 22 Ω resistor array
RN3.what: Series resistors on the USB data lines, as the USB spec asks.

RN4.name: 1 kΩ resistor array
RN4.what: Feeds the ON LED, and links the 16U2's serial lines to D0 and D1 so a shield can still use those pins.

Z1.name: Varistor on D+
Z1.what: Soaks up static discharges on the USB data line.

Z2.name: Varistor on D−
Z2.what: The same guard on the other data line.

L.name: L LED
L.what: The built-in LED on pin 13, through a buffer so it never loads the pin.

TX.name: TX LED
TX.what: Flickers while the board sends serial data to the computer.

RX.name: RX LED
RX.what: Flickers while the computer sends data to the board.

ON.name: ON LED
ON.what: Green, lit whenever the 5 V rail is up.

RESET.name: RESET button
RESET.what: Pulls the 328P's reset low while you hold it. Release it and the bootloader runs, then your sketch.

JP2.name: 16U2 spare pins
JP2.what: Four unused 16U2 pins brought out to pads. No header is fitted.

RESET-EN.name: RESET-EN jumper
RESET-EN.what: A trace between two pads. Cut it and opening the serial port no longer resets the board (uploads then need a timed press of RESET).

ICSP1.name: ICSP header for the 16U2
ICSP1.what: Six pins for programming the USB bridge chip directly.

ICSP.name: ICSP header for the 328P
ICSP.what: Six pins carrying SPI (D11, D12, D13), 5 V, GND and RESET, for a programmer or an SPI shield.

X2.name: USB-B socket
X2.what: Power and data from your computer, through one cable.

X1.name: Barrel jack
X1.what: 2.1 mm, centre positive, for a 7-12 V adapter or battery pack.

IOH.name: Digital header D8-D13
IOH.what: D8-D13, GND, AREF and the I²C pins SDA and SCL.

IOL.name: Digital header D0-D7
IOL.what: D0-D7. D0 and D1 are the serial pins the USB bridge also uses.

POWER.name: Power header
POWER.what: IOREF, RESET, 3.3V, 5V, two GND and VIN.

AD.name: Analog header A0-A5
AD.what: Six analog inputs, read with analogRead() as 0-1023.

led.note: Anode (long leg) toward the pin, cathode to GND, with a 220 Ω to 1 kΩ resistor in series.
led.caution: Never without the resistor: the pin would try to push over 100 mA through the LED.

push-button.note: Between D2 and GND with pinMode(2, INPUT_PULLUP): reads LOW while pressed. With an external pull-down to GND and the button to 5 V it reads HIGH while pressed instead.

potentiometer.note: Ends to GND and 5V, the middle leg (wiper) to A0. analogRead(A0) then goes from 0 to 1023 as you turn it.

ldr.note: From 5V to A0, with a 10 kΩ resistor from A0 to GND. More light, lower resistance, higher reading.

piezo-buzzer.note: + to a pin, − to GND. tone(pin, frequency) plays a note; a piezo draws only a few mA, so no resistor is needed.

tmp36.note: Flat face toward you: left leg 5V, middle leg to A0, right leg GND. Degrees C = (volts − 0.5) × 100.

servo-sg90.note: Brown to GND, red to 5V, orange to a pin (D9). Servo.attach(9) then write(0..180).
servo-sg90.caution: A moving servo can draw 250 mA and a stalled one 700 mA. More than one servo needs its own 5 V supply, with the grounds joined.

tip120.note: Base through a 1 kΩ resistor to a PWM pin, emitter to GND, the load from 5 V (or its own supply) to the collector.
tip120.caution: A motor or fan needs a 1N4007 diode across it, band toward the + supply, or switching it off sends a voltage spike into the transistor.

hc-sr04.note: VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TRIG to D9, ECHO to D10. A 10 µs pulse on TRIG starts a ping; ECHO's pulse length is the round trip.

ssd1306.note: GND, VCC to 3V3, SCL to SCL, SDA to SDA. The display answers at I²C address 0x3C.
ssd1306.caution: Check your module: many SSD1306 boards are 3.3 V only. Ones with an on-board regulator also take 5 V.

uln2003.note: IN1-IN4 to D8-D11, − to GND, + to 5V; the stepper's 5-wire plug goes into the white socket.
uln2003.caution: The stepper takes up to 160 mA with two coils on. Fine from USB for one small stepper; give anything bigger its own supply.

soil-moisture.note: AOUT to A0, VCC to 5V, GND to GND. The reading falls as the soil gets wetter.

traffic-light.note: GND to GND, R to D4, Y to D3, G to D2. The module has its own resistors, so the pins drive it directly.

fsr402.note: One leg to 5V, the other to A0, with a 10 kΩ pull-down from A0 to GND. Press harder, read higher.

mpu6050.note: VCC, GND, SCL to SCL, SDA to SDA. It answers at address 0x68 (0x69 with AD0 high).
mpu6050.caution: Use a breakout with a regulator on it (the common GY-521 has one); the bare chip is 3.3 V only.

pca9685.note: VCC to 5V for its logic, GND, SCL and SDA. It drives up to 16 servos at address 0x40.
pca9685.caution: Feed the servos through the board's V+ terminal from their own 5-6 V supply, never from the Uno's 5V pin.

reverse-jack.title: Adapter with the wrong polarity
reverse-jack.symptom: Nothing at all: the ON LED stays dark and nothing gets warm.
reverse-jack.explanation: The barrel jack goes through D1 before anything else. Reversed, the diode blocks, so no current flows and nothing is harmed. This is exactly what D1 is for.
reverse-jack.fix: Use a centre-positive adapter (the symbol on its label shows + in the middle). The board works straight away; nothing needs replacing.

reverse-vin.title: Reversed supply on the VIN pin
reverse-vin.symptom: Nothing runs, and the regulator near the jack gets hot. The capacitor beside it may bulge or smell.
reverse-vin.explanation: The VIN pin is after D1, so there is no protection on it. A reversed battery drives current backwards through the NCP1117 (U1) and the 47 µF capacitor PC1, which both fail.
reverse-vin.fix: Disconnect at once. Replace U1 and PC1, or run the board from USB if U1 failed open. Feed VIN from the barrel jack instead, where D1 protects it.

brownout.title: Motor on the 5V pin
brownout.symptom: The sketch keeps restarting: the L LED flashes the bootloader pattern again and again, and the Serial Monitor prints the setup banner over and over.
brownout.explanation: A motor starting takes close to an amp. USB's polyfuse and the cable can't supply that, so the 5 V rail sags below 2.7 V and the 328P's brown-out detector holds it in reset until the voltage recovers.
brownout.fix: Give the motor its own supply, switch it with a transistor, and join the grounds. Never run a motor from the 5V pin.

overvoltage.title: 24 V on the barrel jack
overvoltage.symptom: The board dies and the regulator gets too hot to touch. If the regulator fails short, the ON LED may glow bright for a moment before everything stops.
overvoltage.explanation: The NCP1117 is rated to 20 V in. At 24 V it fails, and a regulator that fails short passes the input straight to the 5 V rail, which takes the 328P and the 16U2 with it.
overvoltage.fix: Use 7-12 V on the jack. 9 V is ideal: the regulator has room to work and doesn't get hot.

undervoltage.title: Batteries nearly flat
undervoltage.symptom: The board keeps resetting and the ON LED is dim. It ran fine on fresh batteries yesterday.
undervoltage.explanation: Four AA cells make 6 V fresh but about 4.4 V nearly flat. After D1's 0.7 V and the regulator's 1.1 V dropout, only about 2.6 V reaches the 5 V rail: below the 328P's 2.7 V brown-out level, so it is held in reset.
undervoltage.fix: Use fresh batteries or 6 AA cells (9 V), or power it from USB. The jack needs at least 7 V for a steady 5 V.

pin5-overvoltage.title: 9 V on the 5V pin
pin5-overvoltage.symptom: A hot smell, and the board is dead. The 328P may be hot to the touch.
pin5-overvoltage.explanation: The 5V pin is the 5 V rail itself. 9 V there skips the regulator and lands on every chip on the board; the 328P and the 16U2 are rated to 6 V at most.
pin5-overvoltage.fix: Put 7-12 V on VIN or the jack, never on 5V. The 328P is socketed, so swap it; a dead 16U2 needs soldering.

cold-usb.title: Cold joint on the USB socket
cold-usb.symptom: The board resets when you touch the cable, the ON LED flickers and the serial port comes and goes.
cold-usb.explanation: A joint that never wetted properly is a dull, grainy blob with a crack under it. It touches some of the time, so the 5 V from USB comes and goes.
cold-usb.fix: Reflow the socket's pins with fresh flux until each joint is a shiny cone, then check the board stays up while you wiggle the cable.

missing-resonator.title: No resonator for the 328P
missing-resonator.symptom: The ON LED lights, but nothing runs: L stays dark and every upload fails with "not in sync".
missing-resonator.explanation: The 328P is set to run from an external 16 MHz clock. Without Y2 it has no clock at all, so it never executes an instruction, not even the bootloader.
missing-resonator.fix: Unplug, fit a 16 MHz resonator at Y2, and solder it.

missing-autoreset.title: No auto-reset capacitor
missing-autoreset.symptom: The sketch runs, but uploads fail with "not in sync" unless you press RESET at just the right moment.
missing-autoreset.explanation: C5 turns the 16U2's DTR signal into a short reset pulse. Without it, opening the port no longer restarts the 328P, so the bootloader never gets its chance to listen for the upload.
missing-autoreset.fix: Fit a 100 nF capacitor at C5. Until then, press RESET just as the IDE says "Uploading".

chip-backwards.title: The 328P in its socket backwards
chip-backwards.symptom: Nothing runs, the chip gets hot within seconds, and the USB port may complain about too much current.
chip-backwards.explanation: Turned round, the chip's power pins land on the wrong rails: 5 V reaches pins that should be GND. Current pours through the chip's protection diodes and it overheats.
chip-backwards.fix: Unplug at once. Put the chip back with its notch toward the ICSP header, matching the notch printed on the board. If it got hot, try a new one.

cap-backwards.title: 5 V capacitor fitted backwards
cap-backwards.symptom: A pop, a fishy smell and a bulging capacitor. Afterwards the board may still run, but resets easily under load.
cap-backwards.explanation: An electrolytic capacitor only works one way round. Reversed, the oxide layer inside breaks down, it heats up and its vent splits.
cap-backwards.fix: Unplug, replace PC2 with the black band on the side marked − on the board, and clean any electrolyte off.

short-5v.title: 5V shorted to GND
short-5v.symptom: The board goes dark at once and the polyfuse gets warm. Your computer may warn that the USB device draws too much power.
short-5v.explanation: A wire or a solder bridge from 5V to GND draws as much current as USB can give. The polyfuse F1 heats up and goes high-resistance, cutting the supply to protect your computer's port.
short-5v.fix: Unplug and find the short (a stray jumper on the breadboard rails is the usual one). F1 recovers on its own after a minute.

short-3v3.title: 3V3 shorted to GND
short-3v3.symptom: Anything on 3V3 goes dead. On a real Uno the rest of the board keeps running; this figure's model shuts the whole supply off instead.
short-3v3.explanation: The LP2985 limits its own current and shuts down when it gets too hot, so a short on 3V3 kills the 3.3 V pin but leaves the 5 V rail alone.
short-3v3.fix: Remove the short. The regulator recovers by itself once it cools.

led-no-resistor.title: LED with no resistor
led-no-resistor.symptom: The LED flashes very bright once, then stays dark for good. D13 may be weaker afterwards.
led-no-resistor.explanation: Without a resistor, only the pin's own driver limits the current: about (5 − 2) V ÷ 26 Ω ≈ 115 mA, far past the LED's 20 mA and the pin's 40 mA maximum.
led-no-resistor.fix: Put a 220 Ω resistor in series with every LED and replace the burnt one. Pick 220 Ω again to clear it here.

unplug.title: Unplug it
unplug.body: Pull the USB cable and the adapter. Never build or repair a live board.

strip.title: Strip to the bare PCB
strip.body: Take every part off. What is left is the bare teal circuit board with its pads, silkscreen and the two solder jumpers.
strip.refusal: Unplug the power first: never work on a live board.

pick-place.title: Pick and place, then reflow
pick-place.body: A machine dabs solder paste on the pads, sets down every surface-mount part (the 16U2, regulators, resistors, capacitors, LEDs, the resonator and the RESET button), and the board rides through a reflow oven that melts the paste.
pick-place.refusal: Surface-mount parts go first, before anything plastic that the oven would melt.

place-sk1.title: The DIP-28 socket
place-sk1.body: The socket goes in first among the through-hole parts. Its notch matches the one printed on the board, toward the ICSP header.

place-low.refusal: Surface-mount parts and the reflow come first.

place-y1.title: The 16 MHz crystal
place-y1.body: Y1 is a through-hole HC-49/S crystal for the 16U2, so it goes in now with the other low parts, not with the reflowed ones.

place-icsp.title: The 328P's ICSP header
place-icsp.body: Six pins in two rows near the right edge.

place-icsp1.title: The 16U2's ICSP header
place-icsp1.body: Six pins next to the USB socket, for flashing the bridge chip.

place-x2.title: The USB-B socket
place-x2.body: Tall parts go in after the low ones, so the board lies flat while you solder.

place-tall.refusal: Low parts first: with tall parts in, the board rocks and the low ones fall out when you turn it over to solder.

place-x1.title: The barrel jack
place-x1.body: Its three tabs go through slots in the board.

place-power.title: The power header
place-power.body: Eight female sockets: NC, IOREF, RESET, 3.3V, 5V, GND, GND, VIN.

place-ad.title: The analog header
place-ad.body: Six female sockets, A0 to A5.

place-ioh.title: The D8-D13 header
place-ioh.body: Ten female sockets: D8-D13, GND, AREF, SDA and SCL.

place-iol.title: The D0-D7 header
place-iol.body: Eight female sockets. The gap between the two top headers makes shields fit only one way.

solder.title: Solder the through-hole joints
solder.body: Turn the board over and solder every pin. A good joint is a shiny cone that wets both the pad and the pin.
solder.refusal: Place a part first: there is nothing to solder yet.

chip.title: Press in the ATmega328P
chip.body: Last of all, the chip goes into its socket, notch toward the ICSP header. Soldering is finished, so the chip never sees the iron.
chip.refusal: Solder everything first. Never heat a chip sitting in its socket.

plug.title: Plug in USB
plug.body: The ON LED lights at once. Your computer finds a new serial port called "Arduino Uno", and the stored sketch starts.

upload.title: Upload a sketch
upload.body: The 16U2 pulses DTR, C5 resets the 328P, the bootloader flashes L three times and takes the new program. RX and TX flicker while it goes over.
upload.refusal: Plug in USB first: uploads go over the cable.

power-check.title: Check the power
power-check.body: ON is lit, the 5V pin reads 5.0 V and the 3V3 pin 3.3 V. The Serial Monitor at 9600 baud prints "hello from the Uno" once a second.

break-chip.title: Break it: chip in backwards
break-chip.body: Unplug, then turn the 328P round in its socket.

power-chip.title: Plug in and watch
power-chip.body: Within seconds the chip is hot and nothing runs. Unplug fast on a real board.

fix-chip.title: Put it back the right way
fix-chip.body: Unplug and turn the chip round, notch toward the ICSP header.

break-resonator.title: Break it: take out the resonator
break-resonator.body: Unplug, then remove Y2 with hot air.

power-resonator.title: Plug in and watch
power-resonator.body: The ON LED lights, but L stays dark: with no clock the 328P never runs a single instruction.

break-brownout.title: Break it: a motor on 5V
break-brownout.body: A motor on the 5V pin drags the rail down at every start. Watch the status flip to brown-out and the sketch restart.

exploded.title: Exploded view
exploded.body: Unplug, then lift every layer apart: surface-mount parts, low parts, tall parts and the chip in its socket.

board.title: Meet the Uno
board.lede: Before any wiring, get to know the board: where power comes in, which pins do what, and the little L LED on pin 13 that your first sketch will light.

checks.1: The sketch runs for 3 seconds without an error
checks.2: D13 is HIGH half a second in, so L is lit
checks.3: pin 13 is set as an output with pinMode()

D0-D13.role: HIGH (5 V) or LOW (0 V), in or out. The ~ ones can also do PWM.

5V-3V3.role: 5 V and 3.3 V for sensors and modules.

GND.role: The 0 V every circuit returns to. All the GND pins are joined.

VIN.role: 7-12 V in, or the jack's voltage out.

RESET.role: Pull it LOW to restart the sketch.

callouts.X2: USB: power and uploads through one cable.
callouts.ZU4: The ATmega328P: your sketch runs here.
callouts.IOL: Digital pins 0-7. 0 and 1 are the serial pins.
callouts.X1: Barrel jack for a 7-12 V adapter.
callouts.POWER: 5V, 3.3V, GND and VIN for your circuits.

8.label: Power
8.value: USB 5 V, or 7-12 V on the jack or VIN

features.1: Click any part of the board to see what it does
features.2: Every pin, labelled the way the silkscreen prints it
features.3: Toggle the chip to make L blink, then Run

steps.1: Find the USB socket and the barrel jack on the left: those are the two ways in for power.
steps.2: The long black chip in the socket is the ATmega328P. Your code runs there.
steps.3: Along the top edge are the digital pins; along the bottom, power and the analog inputs.
steps.4: Press Run. setup() makes pin 13 an output and loop() sets it HIGH: the L LED beside pin 13 lights.
steps.5: Turn on the blink chip and run again: now loop() turns L off as well, once a second.

hints.1: LED_BUILTIN is just another name for 13 on the Uno.
hints.2: Without a delay() after LOW, the LED would be off for only a few microseconds: too short to see.

options.2: The ATmega16U2 near the USB socket

q1.why: The 328P runs the sketch. The 16U2 is only the USB-to-serial bridge.

q2.q: What voltage does a HIGH digital pin put out on the Uno?
q2.why: The Uno is a 5 V board: HIGH is 5 V, LOW is 0 V.

q3.q: Which pins can do PWM with analogWrite()?
q3.why: Only 3, 5, 6, 9, 10 and 11 have a timer output behind them; the silkscreen marks them with ~.

q4.q: What happens if you plug in an adapter with the wrong polarity on the barrel jack?
q4.why: The jack goes through a protection diode, D1, which blocks a reversed supply. The VIN pin has no such protection.

blink.title: Blink an LED
blink.lede: Your first circuit: an LED and a resistor on the breadboard, driven by pin 13. Change the timing and the resistor and see what each does.

resistor.label: Resistor
resistor.220-note: About 14 mA: bright, and safe for the LED and the pin.
resistor.1000-note: About 3 mA: dimmer, still easy to see.

checks.1: The sketch runs for 8 seconds without an error
checks.2: D13 turns on and off at least twice, 50 ms to 2 s per cycle
checks.3: LED_PIN is an output and the code turns it off again

D13.to: Resistor, then the LED's long leg
D13.role: Switches the LED: HIGH lights it.

GND.role: Where the current goes back to.

callouts.LED1: Long leg (anode) toward the resistor, short leg to GND.
callouts.IOH: D13 and the GND beside it.
callouts.RES1: Limits the current. Without it the LED burns out.
callouts.L: The built-in LED blinks along: it is on pin 13 too.

features.1: Run it and watch both LEDs blink
features.2: Swap the resistor and see the brightness change
features.3: Break it: take the resistor out in Break it

steps.1: Follow the wire from D13 into the breadboard: it reaches the resistor, then the LED's long leg.
steps.2: Press Run. The breadboard LED and L blink together, half a second on, half a second off.
steps.3: Change On for and Off for, and run again. Try 100 ms on, 900 ms off.
steps.4: Pick 10 kΩ: the LED is barely lit. Less current, less light.

hints.1: An LED only works one way round. If it stays dark, turn it round.
hints.2: Under about 20 ms per blink your eye sees a steady glow instead of flashing.
hints.3: The breadboard's five holes in a column are joined underneath; that is how the resistor and the LED meet.

q1.q: Why does the LED need a resistor?
q1.why: An LED has almost no resistance of its own once it lights. The resistor sets the current: about 14 mA with 220 Ω.

q2.q: With delay(500) after HIGH and delay(500) after LOW, how often does the LED blink?
q2.why: One full cycle is 500 ms on plus 500 ms off: one second.

button.title: Push a button
button.lede: An input at last: a push button on D2 decides when the LED on D13 lights. Hold it to light the LED, or switch the code so each press toggles it.

code.last: the reading from the last loop
code.input: the 10 kΩ pull-down holds D2 LOW

logic.label: Button does
logic.hold-note: The LED copies the button: on while you press.
logic.toggle-note: Each new press flips the LED. The 30 ms wait rides out the contact bounce.

checks.1: D13 goes HIGH within 60 ms of the first press
checks.2: The LED is on while the button is held
checks.3: The LED is off again at the end
checks.4: The code reads the button with digitalRead()

D2.to: The other side of the button, and the 10 kΩ pull-down
D2.role: Reads HIGH while pressed, LOW otherwise.

GND.role: Holds D2 LOW when the button is up, and returns the LED's current.

callouts.BTN1: Pressing joins column 8 (5 V) to column 10 (D2).
callouts.RES1: Pull-down: without it D2 floats and reads at random.
callouts.IOL: D2 is on the right-hand header.

features.1: Press the button in the figure while the code runs
features.2: Why a floating input reads nonsense
features.3: Hold or toggle: one chip changes the logic

steps.1: Follow 5V to one side of the button and D2 to the other. The 10 kΩ resistor ties D2 to GND.
steps.2: Press Run, then press and hold the button: the LED lights while you hold it.
steps.3: Switch Button does to Toggle on each press and run again: now every press flips the LED.
steps.4: Watch the code: toggling only happens when the reading goes from LOW to HIGH, so holding the button does nothing more.

hints.1: Take the pull-down out and D2 picks up noise from your finger: the LED flickers on its own.
hints.2: Contacts bounce for a few ms. Without the 30 ms wait, one press can toggle the LED several times.
hints.3: INPUT_PULLUP would let you skip the resistor, but then pressed reads LOW.

q1.q: What does the 10 kΩ resistor do?

options.1: Holds D2 LOW while the button is up

q1.why: It is a pull-down. Without it D2 is connected to nothing when the button is up, and an unconnected input reads at random.

q2.q: In toggle mode, why does the code compare now with last?

options.3: To react only to the moment of pressing

q2.why: now == HIGH and last == LOW is true only in the loop where the press starts, so a held button toggles once.

knob.title: Turn a knob
knob.lede: A potentiometer turns its position into a voltage, analogRead() turns that into 0-1023, and analogWrite() sets the LED's brightness to match.

checks.1: It prints the starting reading, 620, at least 5 times in the first second
checks.2: At 620 the LED's PWM duty is about 61 %
checks.3: Turned fully clockwise (1023), D9 is fully on
checks.4: Turned fully anticlockwise (0), D9 is off

5V.role: The top of the voltage divider.

callouts.POT1: The wiper slides along a carbon track between 0 V and 5 V.
callouts.IOH: D9 is a ~ pin, so it can do PWM.

2.label: analogRead()
2.value: 0-1023 for 0-5 V, about 4.9 mV per step

features.1: Turn the knob in the figure while it runs
features.2: The same number in the Serial Monitor and on the LED

steps.1: The knob's outer legs go to 5V and GND; its middle leg goes to A0.
steps.2: Press Run and open the Serial Monitor: it prints 620, the knob's starting position.
steps.3: Turn the knob clockwise: the number climbs toward 1023 and the LED gets brighter.
steps.4: Change Read every to 500 ms: the readings come slower, and so does the LED's response.

hints.1: analogWrite() is not a real analog voltage: it switches the pin on and off 490 times a second, and the duty sets the brightness.
hints.2: If turning clockwise makes the reading fall, the 5V and GND legs are swapped. Either is fine; the code just reads the other way.

q1.q: Why does the code divide the reading by 4?

options.3: Because the LED needs a quarter of the current

q1.why: The ADC has 10 bits and PWM has 8. 1023 ÷ 4 ≈ 255.

q2.q: Which pin could not replace D9 for the LED's brightness?
q2.why: D8 has no ~: analogWrite() there can only switch it fully on or off.

rgb.title: Mix colours
rgb.lede: An RGB LED is three LEDs in one: red, green and blue. Give each its own PWM pin and mix any colour from three numbers.

checks.1: Red on D9 runs at 170 of 255, about 67 %
checks.3: Blue on D11 is fully on

GND.role: Common cathode: all three colours return here.

callouts.LED1: Common cathode: the longest leg goes to GND.
callouts.IOH: D9, D10 and D11 are all ~ pins.
callouts.RES1: Each colour gets its own resistor.

2.label: Forward voltage
2.value: Red about 2 V, green and blue about 3 V

5.label: PWM
5.value: About 490 Hz on all three pins

features.2: Why each leg needs its own resistor
features.3: Run it and read the colour off the LED

steps.1: Find the RGB LED's longest leg: it goes to GND. The other three are red, green and blue.
steps.2: Press Run: red at 170 and blue at 255 make purple.
steps.3: Set all three to 255 for white, or all to 0 for off.
steps.4: Try red 255, green 80, blue 0 for orange.

hints.1: If the colours are inverted, you have a common-anode LED: its common leg goes to 5V and 255 means off.
hints.2: Green looks brighter than red at the same number: your eye is most sensitive to green.

q1.q: Red 255, green 255, blue 0. What colour is that?
q1.why: Light mixes by adding: red plus green makes yellow.

q2.q: Why can't the RGB LED share one resistor between its three colours?

options.1: The colours have different forward voltages, so one would hog the current

q2.why: Red lights at about 2 V, green and blue at about 3 V. On one shared resistor, red takes most of the current.

light.title: Sense light
light.lede: A light-dependent resistor and a 10 kΩ resistor make a voltage divider. When the room gets dark, the reading drops and the LED comes on, like a night light.

checks.1: It prints a reading at least 10 times
checks.2: In the starting room light the LED is off
checks.3: Cover the sensor and the LED lights within 150 ms
checks.4: With the lamp back on, the LED goes off again

A0.to: Between the LDR and the 10 kΩ resistor
A0.role: Reads higher as the light gets brighter.

D9.role: Lights the LED when it is dark.

callouts.LDR1: Its resistance falls as light hits it: about 1 MΩ in the dark, a few kΩ in daylight.

1.label: LDR
1.value: GL5528 type, roughly 10 kΩ at 10 lux

features.1: How a voltage divider turns resistance into a reading
features.2: Dim the lamp and watch the LED come on
features.3: Tune the threshold for your room

steps.1: The LDR runs from 5V to A0; the 10 kΩ resistor runs from A0 to GND.
steps.2: Press Run and open the Serial Monitor: in normal light it reads around 770.
steps.3: Turn the lamp down to almost nothing: the reading falls below 400 and the LED lights.
steps.4: Move Dark below to change where the LED switches on.

hints.1: If the reading goes down as the light goes up, the LDR and the resistor have swapped places.
hints.2: Near the threshold the LED can flicker. Two thresholds, one to switch on and a higher one to switch off, fix that.

q1.q: Why is the 10 kΩ resistor there?

options.1: It makes a voltage divider with the LDR so A0 sees a changing voltage

q1.why: analogRead() measures voltage, not resistance. The divider turns the LDR's changing resistance into a changing voltage.

q2.q: The room gets darker. What happens to the reading?
q2.why: In the dark the LDR's resistance rises, so less of the 5 V reaches A0.

distance.title: Measure distance
distance.lede: The HC-SR04 sends a burst of ultrasound and times the echo. Sound travels about 1 cm every 29 µs, so the round trip in microseconds ÷ 58 gives centimetres.

code.ping: a 10 µs pulse starts a measurement
code.echo: echo time in µs ÷ 58 = distance in cm

obstacle.label: Obstacle
obstacle.car-note: Hard and flat at the front: a clean echo.
obstacle.box-note: A big flat face: the easiest target.
obstacle.ball-note: Curved, so much of the sound bounces away.
obstacle.wall-note: Always there: good for checking the range.

checks.1: At the start it reads 30 cm at least 5 times within a second
checks.2: Move the obstacle to 12 cm and it reads 12 cm
checks.4: Out of range, the echo times out and it prints 0 cm
checks.5: The code times the echo with pulseIn()

D9.role: A 10 µs HIGH pulse starts a ping.

D10.role: Stays HIGH as long as the sound is in flight.

callouts.US1: One transducer sends, the other listens.
callouts.IOH: TRIG on D9, ECHO on D10.
callouts.OBST: Move it to change the distance.

features.2: What pulseIn() returns when nothing echoes
features.3: Move the obstacle while it measures

steps.1: Wire VCC to 5V, GND to GND, TRIG to D9 and ECHO to D10.
steps.2: Press Run and open the Serial Monitor: it reads 30 cm.
steps.3: Drag the obstacle closer and further: the numbers follow.
steps.4: Move it out of range: pulseIn() gives up after 30 ms and returns 0.

hints.1: Sound covers 1 cm in about 29 µs; there and back is 58 µs per cm.
hints.2: Soft or angled things like curtains and balls scatter the sound and read badly.
hints.3: Wait at least 60 ms between pings so the last echo has died away.

q1.q: The echo pulse is 1160 µs long. How far away is the obstacle?

q2.q: Why does the code print 0 cm when nothing is in front?

options.1: pulseIn() times out after 30 ms and returns 0
options.3: The Uno cannot count that high

q2.why: The third argument, 30000, is a timeout in µs. With no echo, pulseIn() returns 0.

sound.title: Play a tune
sound.lede: tone() makes a square wave at any frequency on any pin. Put a piezo buzzer on D8, give it a list of notes, and it plays a tune.

code.count: how many notes are in the list
code.gap: a short gap so repeated notes sound separate

tune.label: Tune
tune.scale-note: C4 up to C5, eight notes.
tune.twinkle-note: The first line, starting on middle C.

checks.1: The first note is middle C, 262 Hz
checks.2: The third note is G, 392 Hz
checks.3: The code plays notes with tone()

D8.role: tone() drives it with a square wave.

callouts.BUZ1: A passive piezo: it only sounds when driven with a frequency.
callouts.ZU4: Timer 2 inside the 328P makes the tone.

5.label: Timer
5.value: tone() uses timer 2, which also runs PWM on D3 and D11

features.1: Pick a tune and hear it
features.2: Why every note in an octave doubles

steps.1: Wire the buzzer's + leg to D8 and its − leg to GND.
steps.2: Press Run: Twinkle, Twinkle plays, then a one-second pause, then again.
steps.3: Switch Tune to Ode to Joy, and change Note length to speed it up.
steps.4: Edit the numbers in melody[]: 523 is the C an octave above 262.

hints.1: While tone() is playing, analogWrite() on D3 and D11 stops working: they share timer 2.
hints.2: Without the extra 50 ms, two equal notes in a row would merge into one long note.

q1.q: Middle C is 262 Hz. What is the C an octave higher?
q1.why: Each octave doubles the frequency: 262 × 2 = 524 Hz. The tune uses 523, the exact value.

options.2: The number of notes in the list

q2.why: sizeof(melody) is the array's size in bytes; dividing by the size of one int gives how many there are.

piano.title: Build a piano
piano.lede: Eight buttons on D2-D9, one buzzer on D10. The internal pull-ups save eight resistors, and the sketch plays whichever key is down.

code.playing: which key is sounding; −1 means none
code.pullup: the 328P's own pull-up: no resistor needed
code.down: with a pull-up, pressed reads LOW

octave.label: Octave
octave.c5-note: One octave higher: every frequency doubled.

checks.5: The keys use INPUT_PULLUP and the buzzer stops with noTone()

D2-D9.role: Pulled up inside the chip; a press pulls the pin to GND.

GND.to: The other side of every key, and the buzzer
GND.role: The ground rail along the top of the breadboard.

callouts.KEY1: The lowest note. Each key joins its pin to GND.
callouts.BUZ1: One buzzer: only one note at a time.
callouts.IOL: D2-D7 here, D8 and D9 on the next header.

4.label: Notes at once
4.value: 1: tone() drives one pin at a time

features.2: Pull-ups turn the logic upside down
features.3: Why only one note sounds at once

steps.1: Each key sits across the breadboard's gap: one side to a pin from D2 to D9, the other to the GND rail.
steps.2: Press Run and click the keys: the buzzer plays and the Serial Monitor prints the note.
steps.3: Switch Octave to C5 to C6: the same keys, an octave higher.
steps.4: Hold two keys: the higher one wins, because the loop keeps the last pressed key it finds.

hints.1: If every key sounds all the time, the pins are set to INPUT instead of INPUT_PULLUP: they float.
hints.2: The sketch only calls tone() when the key changes. Calling it every loop restarts the note and makes it buzz.

q1.q: With INPUT_PULLUP, what does an unpressed key read?
q1.why: The internal resistor pulls the pin up to 5 V. Only a press pulls it down to LOW.

q2.q: Why don't the keys need their own resistors?

options.3: The 328P has pull-up resistors built in

q2.why: INPUT_PULLUP switches on a 20-50 kΩ resistor inside the chip for each pin.

motor.title: Drive a motor
motor.lede: A motor needs far more current than a pin can give. A TIP120 transistor does the heavy lifting, PWM on D6 sets the speed, and a diode catches the spike when the motor stops.

code.pin: D6 is a ~ pin, so it can do PWM

checks.1: One second in, the motor is at about half speed
checks.2: At 2.6 s it runs at full speed

D6.to: 1 kΩ resistor, then the transistor's base

5V.to: The motor's + lead and the diode

callouts.Q1: TIP120 Darlington: a few mA on its base switches up to 5 A.
callouts.RES1: 1 kΩ: limits the base current to about 3 mA.
callouts.DIO1: Flyback diode: soaks up the voltage spike when the motor turns off.
callouts.MOT1: A small DC motor: speed follows the PWM duty.

4.label: Motor current
4.value: 100-500 mA, far over a pin's 20 mA

features.1: Watch it speed up, run and stop
features.2: How a small current switches a big one
features.3: Leave out the diode and the spike can kill the transistor

steps.1: D6 goes through the 1 kΩ resistor to the TIP120's base. The motor sits between 5V and the collector; the emitter goes to GND.
steps.2: The diode is across the motor, pointing toward 5V.
steps.3: Press Run: the motor speeds up over about two seconds, runs at full speed, then stops.
steps.4: Lower Top speed or raise Speed-up step and run again.

hints.1: Below about 30 % duty a small motor may hum but not turn: it needs a push to overcome friction.
hints.2: A real motor should run from its own supply, sharing only GND with the Uno. USB's 500 mA runs out fast.

q1.q: Why not wire the motor straight to D6?

options.1: It needs far more current than a pin can give

q1.why: A pin is safe to 20 mA; a small motor draws hundreds. The transistor switches the motor's current.

q2.q: What does the diode across the motor do?

options.3: Catches the voltage spike when it switches off

q2.why: A motor's coil keeps current flowing for a moment when switched off. The diode gives it a path instead of a high-voltage spike.

heat.title: Keep it cool
heat.lede: A TMP36 turns temperature into a voltage. The sketch converts it to degrees and switches on a fan through a transistor when it gets too warm.

code.fan: the fan runs through the TIP120, like the motor
code.limit: turn the fan on above this
code.degrees: TMP36: 0.5 V at 0 °C, plus 10 mV per °C

mode.label: Fan control
mode.onoff-note: Full speed above the limit, off below it.
mode.ramp-note: Starts at the limit and reaches full speed 8 °C above it.

checks.1: At the start it prints about 21.8 °C
checks.2: At room temperature the fan is off
checks.3: Heat it to 34 °C and the fan runs
checks.4: Back down to 26 °C, the fan stops

5V.role: Powers the sensor, and the fan.

A0.role: Reads the temperature as a voltage.

D6.to: 1 kΩ resistor, then the transistor's base

callouts.TMP1: Flat side facing you: +VS left, VOUT middle, GND right.
callouts.FAN1: A 5 V fan, switched like the motor.
callouts.Q1: TIP120: the pin switches it, it switches the fan.
callouts.DRYER: Blow warm air on the sensor here.

features.1: From ADC reading to degrees in two lines
features.2: Heat the sensor and the fan kicks in
features.3: On-off or speed with the heat

steps.1: The TMP36 has three legs: 5V, A0 and GND. Get it the wrong way round and it gets hot.
steps.2: Press Run and open the Serial Monitor: about 21.8 °C.
steps.3: Point the hair dryer at the sensor: above 30 °C the fan starts.
steps.4: Switch Fan control to Speed with the heat and watch the fan follow the temperature.

hints.1: If it reads over 100 °C or below −40 °C, check that VOUT really goes to A0.
hints.2: Near the limit an on-off fan may chatter on and off. Switching off a degree or two lower stops that.

q1.q: The TMP36 outputs 0.75 V. What temperature is that?

q2.q: Why does the fan go through a transistor?

options.1: A pin can't supply the fan's current

q2.why: A fan draws over 100 mA; a pin is safe only to 20 mA.

servo.title: Sweep a servo
servo.lede: A servo turns to the angle you ask for and holds it. The Servo library sends a pulse every 20 ms: 1 ms wide for 0°, 2 ms for 180°.

code.attach: the servo's signal wire is on D9

checks.1: About 1.1 s in, the arm is near 90° on the way up
checks.3: On the way back it passes 90° again

callouts.SRV1: SG90: a motor, gears and a position sensor in one box.

5.label: Current
5.value: Up to about 700 mA when stalled

features.3: Change the range and the speed

steps.1: Brown to GND, red to 5V, orange to D9.
steps.2: Press Run: the arm sweeps from 0° to 180° and back.
steps.3: Set From to 45 and To to 135 for a narrower sweep.
steps.4: Raise Wait per degree to slow it down.

hints.1: If the board resets as the servo moves, the servo is pulling too much current from USB. Give it its own supply.
hints.2: Many cheap servos can't quite reach 0° or 180° and buzz at the ends. Stay a few degrees inside.

q1.q: What tells the servo which angle to go to?

options.1: The voltage on the red wire

q1.why: Pulse width sets the angle: about 1 ms is 0°, 1.5 ms is 90°, 2 ms is 180°.

q2.q: What does arm.write(90) do if the arm is already at 90°?
q2.why: write() sets a position, not a movement. The servo holds whatever angle it is told.

stepper.title: Spin a prize wheel
stepper.lede: A 28BYJ-48 stepper moves in exact steps, so the sketch knows where the wheel stops. Press the button and it spins, slows down and lands on a random prize.

code.steps: steps per turn: 32 steps × a 63.68:1 gearbox
code.pins: the driver's IN1-IN4 on D8-D11, given in the order 8, 10, 9, 11 so the coils fire in sequence
code.at: the segment under the pointer now
code.speed: turns per minute → steps per second
code.press: Press the button to spin the wheel!
code.target: round only once, from the running total, so the error never adds up
code.run: blocks until the wheel has stopped

checks.1: After a press it prints the prize it landed on
checks.2: D8 steps at least 50 times while the wheel turns
checks.3: The stepper is set up as FULL4WIRE on 8, 10, 9, 11

D8-D11.role: Switch the four coils in turn.

5V.to: The driver board's + and the button

D2.to: The button, with a 10 kΩ pull-down

callouts.DRV1: ULN2003 driver board: four transistors for the four coils.

5.label: Current
5.value: About 240 mA with two coils on

features.1: Why a stepper always knows where it is
features.2: Tune speed and acceleration for a smooth stop
features.3: Press and see where it lands

steps.1: The driver's IN1-IN4 go to D8-D11, its + and − to 5V and GND. The motor plugs into the driver.
steps.2: Press Run, then the button: the wheel speeds up, turns and slows onto a prize.
steps.3: Raise Extra full turns for a longer spin, or lower Acceleration for a slower build-up.
steps.4: Push Top speed past about 20 RPM: the motor starts to miss steps and the wheel lands in the wrong place.

hints.1: If the motor only buzzes, the four pins are in the wrong order. The library wants 8, 10, 9, 11.
hints.2: 2038 steps per turn isn't a whole number of steps per segment. Rounding from the running total keeps the wheel lined up over many spins.
hints.3: random() always gives the same sequence after a reset; randomSeed() with a floating analog pin mixes it up.

q1.q: Why can the sketch know the wheel's position without a sensor?

options.2: Every step turns it by the same small angle, so it counts steps

q1.why: A stepper moves a fixed angle per step. As long as no steps are missed, counting them gives the position.

q2.q: What happens if you ask for more speed than the motor can give?

options.1: It misses steps and loses its place

q2.why: Past its limit the rotor can't keep up with the coils. Steps are lost and the count no longer matches the wheel.

plant.title: Plant monitor
plant.lede: A soil probe says how wet the soil is; an OLED screen shows it as a percentage and a bar, and tells you when to water.

code.wet: the reading in a glass of water

checks.2: When the soil dries to 20 % it prints 20
checks.4: The screen starts at address 0x3C and the sketch draws to it

SCL-SDA.role: I²C: clock and data on two wires.

callouts.SOIL1: Capacitive probe: no bare metal in the soil, so it doesn't corrode.

3.label: Probe output
3.value: About 2.5 V dry, 1.3 V in water

4.label: Screen buffer
4.value: 1 KB of the Uno's 2 KB RAM

5.label: I²C pins
5.value: SDA = A4, SCL = A5 (also by AREF)

features.1: Calibrate with a dry and a wet reading
features.2: Two wires carry everything to the screen
features.3: Water it and watch the bar fill

steps.1: The screen needs four wires: GND, 3V3, SCL and SDA.
steps.2: The probe needs three: 5V, GND and its output to A0.
steps.3: Press Run: the screen shows 40 % and Happy :).
steps.4: Dry the soil out: below 30 % the screen asks for water.
steps.5: Set Dry reading and Wet reading from your own probe: hold it in the air, then in water, and note the numbers.

hints.1: If the screen stays blank, try address 0x3D: some boards use it.
hints.2: The probe reads lower when wetter, so DRY is the bigger number. map() handles the reversed range.

q1.q: How does the Uno talk to the OLED?

options.1: Over I²C, on SDA and SCL

q1.why: I²C sends data on SDA, timed by SCL. Every device on the bus has an address; the screen is 0x3C.

q2.q: The reading is 390, halfway between dry (520) and wet (260). What does the screen show?

force.title: Strength tester
force.lede: Hit the pad: a force-sensing resistor measures how hard, a servo needle swings to show it and holds the best hit, and a bell rings if you hit hard enough.

code.pulldown: must match the resistor on the breadboard
code.hold: hold the best hit for a moment, then follow the pad again
code.ohms: work back from the divider to the sensor's resistance

pulldown.label: Pull-down resistor
pulldown.1000-note: Only hard hits register: good for big forces.
pulldown.10000-note: The usual choice: a light touch to a firm press.
pulldown.100000-note: Very sensitive: a light tap reads near the top.

checks.1: A light press reads 682, about 5000 Ω
checks.3: A hard hit rings the bell at 1568 Hz
checks.4: The needle swings near the top
checks.5: After the hold time it drops back to 0°

A0.to: Between the FSR and the 10 kΩ resistor
A0.role: Reads higher the harder you press.

callouts.METER: The needle shows the best hit.
callouts.FSR1: FSR 402: no press is over 1 MΩ; a hard press is a few hundred Ω.

features.1: Hit it and watch the needle
features.2: How the divider gives you the sensor's resistance
features.3: Pick a pull-down to set the sensitivity
features.4: A peak hold, like a fairground strength tester

steps.1: The FSR runs from 5V to A0, the 10 kΩ resistor from A0 to GND. The servo is on D9 and the buzzer on D8.
steps.2: Press Run and press lightly: the needle rises and the Serial Monitor shows the reading and the sensor's resistance.
steps.3: Hit hard: the needle swings near the top and the bell rings.
steps.4: Let go: the needle holds the best hit for 1.5 s, then drops.

hints.1: An FSR is good for 'harder or softer', not for weighing things: two sensors can differ by 25 %.
hints.2: Change Pull-down resistor in the code only if you change the real resistor too, or the ohms come out wrong.

q1.q: What happens to the FSR's resistance when you press harder?
q1.why: Pressing pushes more conductive particles together: from over 1 MΩ untouched down to a few hundred Ω.

q2.q: What is the rung variable for?

options.2: So it rings once per hit, not every loop

q2.why: Without rung the bell would restart every 20 ms while the needle stays high. It resets once the best drops 100 below the bell.

parking.title: Parking sensor
parking.lede: Put the distance sensor and a traffic light together: green when there is room, yellow when it gets close, red when it's time to stop.

code.lights: exactly one light is on at a time

obstacle.label: Obstacle
obstacle.car-note: Hard and flat at the front: a clean echo.
obstacle.box-note: A big flat face: the easiest target.
obstacle.ball-note: Curved, so much of the sound bounces away.
obstacle.wall-note: Always there: good for checking the range.

checks.1: At 40 cm the green light is on
checks.2: At 20 cm the yellow light is on
checks.3: At 8 cm the red light is on
checks.4: and the green light is off
checks.5: It prints 40 cm at the start

5V-GND.to: The sensor's VCC and GND, and the light's GND

callouts.TL1: Traffic light module with its own resistors.

features.1: Set the distances for your garage
features.2: Why a missing echo shows red
features.3: Drive the car in and watch the lights

steps.1: The sensor is wired as in Measure distance: TRIG on D9, ECHO on D10.
steps.2: The traffic light's R, Y and G go to D4, D3 and D2.
steps.3: Press Run and move the car: green, then yellow below 30 cm, then red at 15 cm.
steps.4: Change Green above and Red at or below to suit your space.

hints.1: A comparison like cm > 30 is true or false: 1 or 0. That is why it can go straight into digitalWrite().
hints.2: Out of range, pulseIn() returns 0, and 0 is below Red at or below: an empty driveway shows red. Treat 0 as far away to fix it.

q1.q: The car is 30 cm away. Which light is on?
q1.why: Green needs more than 30. 30 is above 15 and at most 30: yellow.

q2.q: Why does the module need no resistors on the breadboard?

options.3: They are already on the module

q2.why: The traffic light board has a resistor for each LED, so its pins connect straight to D2-D4.
